                                     PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                        §      PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                     §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                  §                   OF TEXAS

                                     PROJECT NO. 59142

 REVIEW OF ERCOT’S                              §      PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 INTERCONNECTION PROCESSES                      §
 FOR LARGE LOADS
                                                §                   OF TEXAS


COMMENTS OF EOLIC DEVELOPMENT PARTNERS REGARDING APPLICATION
OF PROJECT NO. 58481 FINANCIAL CRITERIA TO BATCH ZERO LOADS UNDER
                              PGRR145

       Eolic Development Partners respectfully submit these comments in Project 58481,

Rulemaking to Implement Large Load Interconnection Standards Under PURA §37.0561 and

Project No. 59142, Review of ERCOT’s Interconnection Processes for Large Loads, regarding the

proposed application of financial commitment criteria from Project No. 58481 (proposed 16 TAC

§25.194) to Batch Zero loads under ERCOT’s Planning Guide Revision Request (“PGRR”) 145.

These comments are directed specifically at how those financial criteria interact with, and should

not be mechanically imported into, the Batch Zero framework being developed in this proceeding.

       Eolic Development Partners is a corporate member of the ERCOT Industrial Consumer

market segment and an active participant in the ERCOT large load interconnection process with

projects at various stages of development in the Batch Zero queue. We have invested years of

development and millions of dollars, all in reliance on the regulatory framework in place at the

time those investments were made. We share the Commission’s interest in ensuring system

reliability and screening out speculative projects. However, the wholesale importation of Project
 No. 58481 financial criteria into Batch Zero, what is intended to be a transitional process for

existing, advanced-stage projects, raises serious concerns that we address below.

                                      I. BACKGROUND

       Eolic Development Partners view Batch Zero not as a new large load intake process, but a

transitional framework designed to organize and study large load interconnection requests that

have been in ERCOT’s queue, many for two or more years. A significant number of these loads

have completed multiple rounds of comprehensive ERCOT-directed load interconnection studies,

executed interconnection agreements (“IAs”) with their transmission and/or distribution service

providers (“TDSPs”), posted contributions in aid of construction (“CIAC”), posted financial

security, executed contracts for the procurement of long lead time equipment, and in some cases

have commenced site construction. These are not speculative loads, they are real projects with

demonstrated financial and development commitment.

       Project No. 58481 and its proposed 16 TAC §25.194 were designed to establish standards

for new large load interconnection requests going forward. The financial commitment standards,

including the $50,000/MW intermediate deposit, new intermediate agreement and interconnection

agreement requirements, and non-refundable interconnection fees, are calibrated to screen new

entrants for seriousness and financial capability. ERCOT’s decision to replicate the draft PFP

language from §25.194 into PGRR145 so that Batch Zero can move forward without waiting for

the Project No. 58481 rulemaking to finish, while understandable from a timing perspective, has

the effect of applying proposed standards designed for new loads to an existing population that has

already satisfied equivalent or more stringent requirements.

       Moreover, Project No. 58481 is still in the Proposal for Publication (“PFP”) stage and has

not been adopted as a final rule. The April 17, 2026, PFP comment deadline and the Commission



                                                Eolic Development Partners’ Comments – Page 2
 Open Meeting on that same date represent a critical inflection point, this is when the Commission

must provide direction to ERCOT before the revision requests and the proposed rule start

diverging. Requiring Batch Zero participants to comply with standards that remain subject to

change introduces unacceptable regulatory uncertainty.

                       II. PREFERRED APPROACH:
            GRANDFATHER EXISTING AGREEMENTS AND FINANCIAL
                 COMMITMENTS FOR BATCH ZERO LOADS

       Eolic Development Partners’ recommendation is that the Commission direct ERCOT to

grandfather existing Planning Guide Section 9.5 agreements, CIAC payments, financial security

deposits, and interconnection agreements for all Batch Zero loads that have already executed such

instruments. This approach is grounded in both practical necessity and sound regulatory policy.

A. A Three-Tier Framework Should Govern Batch Zero Financial Commitments

       Consistent with comments filed by multiple stakeholders in both this proceeding and the

PGRR145 stakeholder process, Eolic Development Partners supports a tiered approach that

recognizes the actual development status of each Batch Zero participant:

       Tier 1 – Base Loads (Loads Not Subject to Additional Study under proposed Planning

Guide §9.2.1.1). Loads that have completed studies and have met legacy Planning Guide §9.5

requirements under either: (a) the legacy Interim Large Load Interconnection Process implemented

by ERCOT on March 25, 2022 (see Market Notice W-A032522-01) where a TDSP developed

Regional Planning Group was submitted to ERCOT on or before April 1, 2026, or (b) the legacy

Planning Guide §9.4 and executed interconnection agreements, funded security, and issued notices

to proceed under legacy Planning Guide §9.5 (proposed in PGRR145 to be renumbered as §9.9

and §9.10), which replaced the previous Interim Large Load Interconnection Process, should be

fully grandfathered. Their existing executed and binding IAs with their TDSP and posting of the



                                               Eolic Development Partners’ Comments – Page 3
 applicable CIAC and/or financial security constitute financial commitments that are functionally

equivalent to, and in many cases more stringent than, what Staff’s draft §25.194 PFP proposes. No

new security posting, interconnection fee, or re-execution of agreements should be required for

these existing IAs which were executed in accordance with the applicable ERCOT requirements

at the time. These loads should be treated as fixed planning inputs and should not be subject to re-

screening, re-evaluation, or displacement.

       Tier 2 – Studied Loads with Prior Executed Agreements. Loads that do not qualify

under proposed Planning Guide §9.2.1.1 as Load Not Subject to Additional Study, but that

otherwise meet the qualifications for proposed Planning Guide §9.2.1.2 as studied loads and have

already executed a binding IA with their TDSP and posted the applicable CIAC and/or financial

security under that agreement should likewise be exempt from new financial requirements.

Requiring these loads to post additional security under either provision of proposed Planning

Guide §9.7 would result in double payment for the same interconnection rights. The TDSP should

attest to ERCOT, by July 24, 2026, that the applicable ILLE has executed an interconnection

agreement and posted the required CIAC and financial security.

       Tier 3 – Loads Without Prior Agreements. Loads that otherwise satisfy PGRR145

criteria to be included in Batch Zero as studied load, but currently lack financial commitment under

proposed provisions of proposed Planning Guide §9.2.1.2(1)(b)(1), should be required to satisfy

new financial commitment criteria under proposed Planning Guide §9.7.1 (Intermediate

Agreements). These loads should, at a minimum, execute a conforming intermediate agreement,

post $/MW financial security and provide other related disclosures as a condition of Batch Zero

inclusion. This is the only tier for which new financial requirements are appropriate.

B. Grandfathering Avoids an Administrative Nightmare and Protects Serious Loads



                                                 Eolic Development Partners’ Comments – Page 4
 The practical benefits of grandfathering are substantial:

       First, grandfathering eliminates the need for Batch Zero base loads and Tier 2 loads to

execute new or amended Letters of Agreement (“LOAs”), intermediate agreements, and

interconnection agreements on a compressed timeline. The typical turnaround time for utilities to

review, negotiate, and execute these agreements is 60 to 90 days, although could be longer. Given

that PGRR145 contemplates a July 10, 2026, eligibility deadline for intermediate agreements and

a July 24, 2026, TDSP attestation deadline, there is a strong probability that many eligible Batch

Zero loads will be unable to sign new intermediate or interconnection agreements through no fault

of their own, simply because the administrative machinery of TDSPs and ERCOT cannot process

the volume of agreements required within the available window.

       Second, grandfathering prevents base loads and other serious loads from losing their

position in the queue because of timeline delays attributable to utilities and ERCOT. These loads

have done everything required of them under the regulatory framework that existed at the time

their IAs were executed. Penalizing them for administrative bottlenecks outside their control is

contrary to the objectives of SB6 and PURA §37.0561, which direct the Commission to support

business development while maintaining system reliability.

       Third, grandfathering eliminates the need for the initial $50,000/MW deposit for base

loads and those Tier 2 loads that have already posted the applicable CIAC and/or security required

under their already existing IAs. These loads have already demonstrated that they are serious and

not speculative. The development criteria already being proposed by ERCOT under PG

§9.2.1.1(1)(d) for projects targeting 2027 energization, including attestations of site preparation,

equipment procurement, and construction progress, provide an additional layer of screening that

renders duplicative financial postings unnecessary.



                                                 Eolic Development Partners’ Comments – Page 5
        Fourth, this approach is consistent with cost-causation principles. As noted by multiple

stakeholders, imposing additional financial obligations on projects that have already funded long-

lead equipment, advanced construction, and posted the applicable TDSP-held security would result

in “double collateralization,” requiring developers to pay twice for the same interconnection rights

without any incremental reliability benefit. In many cases, these advanced state legacy agreements

already have downstream customer contracts with obligations in them that are predicated on the

then-current ERCOT requirements.

                      III. ALTERNATIVE APPROACH:
           IF THE COMMISSION DIRECTS ERCOT TO APPLY §25.194
      CRITERIA TO BATCH ZERO, SPECIFIC SAFEGUARDS ARE NECESSARY

       If the Commission determines that Project No. 58481 financial criteria must apply to Batch

Zero, which is not our preferred outcome and will result in significant disruption for developers,

many of whom already have downstream customer contracts that rely on these existing IAs —

Eolic Development Partners respectfully recommend the following measures to mitigate the

adverse impacts:

A. The $/MW Security Requirement Should Apply Only to Loads That Have Not Already
   Demonstrated Financial Commitment

       Even if draft PFP language for §25.194 is applied to Batch Zero, the ultimate $/MW

financial security requirement should apply only to those loads that have not already executed an

interconnection agreement, posted CIAC, or provided financial security under existing ERCOT

and TDSP processes, i.e., only Tier 3 loads. The purpose of the $/MW requirement is to weed out

speculative loads, ensuring that load customers in the queue are financially committed and

ratepayers protected from stranded costs. Base loads and Tier 2 loads have already passed that test.

They have executed binding agreements, posted millions of dollars in CIAC and financial security,

and, in many cases, funded long-lead equipment and commenced construction. Requiring them to


                                                 Eolic Development Partners’ Comments – Page 6
 post an additional $50,000/MW deposit to prove the very commitment they have already

demonstrated serves no screening function and amounts to a duplicative financial penalty on the

most serious participants in the queue.

       For Tier 3 loads that are required to post the $/MW deposit, the financial security should

be fully refundable up to interconnection agreement stage, after deduction of any expenses

incurred by the utility or ERCOT, if they chose to not move forward, or alternatively should be

credited toward the financial security required under the IA if such a component exists, when they

decide to sign the IA. The financial security should not be treated as a non-refundable

interconnection fee at the intermediate stage. At that stage, the developer has received no study

results, no MW allocation, and no information regarding the feasibility or cost of the

interconnection. Penalizing developers for participating in a process that may yield unfavorable

results is inconsistent with the purpose of the Batch Zero study process and will unnecessarily

harm industrial load customers.

B. Standardized Agreements Must Be Finalized and Distributed Immediately

       If the Commission requires new LOAs (or amendments to existing LOAs), intermediate

agreements, and interconnection agreements for Batch Zero loads, the single most important step

the Commission can take is to direct ERCOT and TDSPs to develop and publish standardized,

Commission-approved agreement templates for both intermediate agreements and interconnection

agreements as early as possible. Today, each TDSP uses its own form of agreement, leading to

prolonged bilateral negotiations that consume weeks or months. A standardized agreement

template, analogous to the Standard Generation Interconnection Agreement (“SGIA”) used for

generator interconnections, would dramatically reduce execution timelines, eliminate unnecessary

negotiation cycles, and ensure uniform treatment of all Batch Zero participants regardless of which



                                                Eolic Development Partners’ Comments – Page 7
 TDSP serves them. The following additional operational steps are critical to ensuring that eligible

loads are not penalized by administrative delays:

       (1) Standardized Agreement Templates. The Commission should direct TDSPs and

ERCOT to develop and publish standardized, Commission-approved templates for both

intermediate agreements and interconnection agreements with a deadline date of May 10, 2026,

for any new large loads that will be required to sign these agreements. This date ensures ILLEs

have at least 60 days to sign these agreements in advance of the July 10, 2026, compliance deadline

for Batch Zero loads. A standardized form, similar to the SGIA model used for generators,

eliminates the protracted bilateral negotiations that currently occur between each ILLE and its

TDSP, compresses execution timelines from months to weeks, and ensures uniform treatment

across all TDSPs. TDSPs cannot begin processing agreements until the form is settled, and every

day of delay in publishing the template reduces the window available for execution.

       (2) Rolling Distribution of Base Load Lists. ERCOT should transmit base load eligibility

determinations to each interconnecting TDSP on a rolling basis, at a minimum, every two weeks.

Upon receipt, TDSPs should immediately reach out to the applicable ILLEs to begin the

LOA/agreement execution process. Doing this on a rolling basis with an administrative cure period

for paperwork cleanup, rather than waiting for a single batch distribution, will spread the

administrative workload and reduce bottleneck risk at the back end. As discussed above, base loads

should directly sign interconnection agreements and are not needed to sign intermediate

agreements.

       (3) 60 Day Execution Window. TDSPs should be given a minimum of 60 days from

receipt of agreement templates to execute agreements with ILLEs. The proposed July 10, 2026,

compliance deadline for intermediate and interconnection agreements and the July 24, 2026, TDSP



                                                Eolic Development Partners’ Comments – Page 8
 attestation deadline in PGRR145 should be adjusted if necessary to ensure this window is

available.

        (4) No Penalty for Utility-Side Delays. If a base load or other eligible load misses a

deadline solely because the TDSP did not initiate or complete the agreement process in time, the

load should not lose its queue position or Batch Zero eligibility. The rule should include a safe

harbor provision protecting ILLEs from consequences of delays attributable to TDSPs or ERCOT.

        These steps will give utilities the 60 days typically required to execute agreements and will

substantially reduce the probability that base loads miss deadlines due to administrative issues that

are not their fault.

C. The 80/20 Forfeiture Structure Must Not Apply to Batch Zero Loads

        The proposed 80/20 forfeiture provision under §25.194(g)(3)–(4) is fundamentally

incompatible with the Batch Zero framework. Under this provision, if an ILLE withdraws after

outstanding costs are covered, only 20% of the remaining security balance is refunded; the

remaining 80% is paid to the TDSP as a rate base offset. This structure penalizes developers for

exercising the rational optionality that the batch study process is designed to provide. An ILLE

that posts $50 million in security, participates in the Batch Zero study, and learns that only a

fraction of its requested capacity is available should not face forfeiture of the vast majority of its

deposit for the rational decision to withdraw. At a minimum, this forfeiture provision should not

apply to Batch Zero participants who withdraw after receiving unfavorable study results. To the

extent the Commission seeks to reduce residential customers’ exposure to potential higher costs

due to transmission upgrades, the non-refundable interconnection fee and reforms to ERCOT’s

transmission cost allocation rules would be more appropriate solutions than penalizing all large

load customers that applied to interconnect to the ERCOT grid.



                                                  Eolic Development Partners’ Comments – Page 9
                                        IV. CONCLUSION

       Batch Zero is a transitional process for existing, advanced-stage loads, not a new-load

intake process. Its financial framework should reflect that reality. Eolic Development Partners’

preferred approach, grandfathering existing agreements and adopting a three-tier financial

commitment framework within PGRR145, ensures that the Commission’s objectives of screening

speculative loads and maintaining system reliability are achieved without imposing duplicative

financial obligations on loads that have already demonstrated their commitment through years of

investment and compliance with existing ERCOT processes.

       If the Commission elects to direct ERCOT to apply §25.194 criteria to Batch Zero, the

safeguards described in Section III above, exempting base loads and Tier 2 loads from the $/MW

deposit, ensuring refundability for Tier 3 deposits, standardizing agreements, rolling TDSP

distribution, and protection from administrative delays, are essential to prevent serious, committed

projects from being penalized by a process that was not designed for them.

       Eolic Development Partners respectfully request that the Commission provide clear

direction on these issues at the April 17, 2026, Open Meeting, so that ERCOT and stakeholders

have the certainty necessary to finalize PGRR145 ahead of the June 1 or 2, 2026, vote by the

ERCOT Board of Directors. Clear and definitive direction will provide the regulatory certainty

necessary for project sponsors and capital providers to continue advancing large-scale

infrastructure in Texas, consistent with the Legislature’s directive in PURA §37.0561 to “support

business development in this state while minimizing the potential for stranded infrastructure costs

and maintaining system reliability.”

Respectfully submitted,

Eolic Development Partners

Date: April 14, 2026

                                               Eolic Development Partners’ Comments – Page 10

C. The 80/20 Forfeiture Structure Must Not Apply to Batch Zero Loads

        The proposed 80/20 forfeiture provision under §25.194(g)(3)-(4) is fundamentally

incompatible with the Batch Zero framework. Under this provision, if an ILLE withdraws after

outstanding costs are covered, only 20% of the remaining security balance is refunded; the

remaining 80% is paid to the TDSP as a rate base offset. This structure penalizes developers for

exercising the rational optionality that the batch study process is designed to provide. An ILLE

that posts $50 million in security, participates in the Batch Zero study, and learns that only a

fraction of its requested capacity is available should not face forfeiture of the vast majority of its

deposit for the rational decision to withdraw. At a minimum, this forfeiture provision should not

apply to Batch Zero participants who withdraw after receiving unfavorable study results. To the

extent the Commission seeks to reduce residential customers' exposure to potential higher costs

due to transmission upgrades, the non-refundable interconnection fee and reforms to ERCOT' s

transmission cost allocation rules would be more appropriate solutions than penalizing all large

load customers that applied to interconnect to the ERCOT grid.

       Batch Zero is a transitional process for existing, advanced-stage loads, not a new-load

intake process. Its financial framework should reflect that reality. Eolic Development Partners'

commitment framework within PGRR145, ensures that the Commission's objectives of screening

financial obligations on loads that have already demonstrated their commitment through years of

investment and compliance with existing ERCOT processes.
